pr_title: kernel: Fix pipe ISR instability issues (#52812)
pr_body:
Fixes #52812 (well, most of it)

This series of commits is an attempt to fix the pipe instability issues raised in issue #52812 (the second and third issues). The issues that I have been able identify related to those boil down to improperly protecting the wait queue from within the pipe routines.

When the working list of pended threads (to read from or write to) is generated, sched_spinlock must be taken to protect the wait queue. Otherwise, an in-opportune timeout can lead to problems.

As there is a gap in time between when that list is generated and when data is copied to/from the previously identified waiting thread, that thread can time out. There are two things that need to be done to avoid problems stemming from this.
    1. Waking the thread must be done safely. That is, it must be explicitly specified and a run-time check to determine if it is still pended must be done before unpending it.
    2. A barrier must be inserted after the thread has been safely unpended so that it spins waiting for the pipe lock, which it can get after the put/get operation that was supposed to wake it finishes. I specify "supposed to" because it could have technically timed out while data was being copied, but since it made it to the "working list" before timing out, I am arguing that it is not really a timeout, but a special processing case.

This set of commits does not address the first of the three issues identified in #52812.

issue_context.title: Various problems with pipes (Not unblocking, Data Access Violation, unblocking wrong thread...)
comments: I'm looking into this right away.

Update on issue 1/3.

Pipes currently have some weird (legacy) quirks. Blame me. This one has to do with interactions between the minimum of bytes to receive, the requested number of bytes to receive and the timeout.  For reference, the documentation for k_pipe_get() currently reads as ... 

> Data is synchronously received from a pipe by a thread. If the specified minimum number of bytes can not be immediately satisfied, then the operation will either fail immediately or attempt to receive as many bytes as possible and then pend in the hope that the receive can be completed later."

There is some ambiguity as to how much data the routine should wait for while pended. The current implementation attempts to wait for all the requested data--not the minimum data; if the timeout finishes before all the requested data has been received then, the return value is set based on how much of the data was received as compared to the minimum requested. This is not the most consistent as sometimes we measure the completeness and success as it compares to the minimum requested and sometimes with total requested. In the case of the first issue (read first, then write) it is waiting forever for all the data and not the minimum data.

I suspect it would ultimately be better to be uniform in our approach and always base both completion and success on the minimum number of bytes transferred. As an aside, this would mean that the simplest way to interpret the bytes_to_read and bytes_to_write parameters of k_pipe_get() and k_pipe_put() would be as maximum values. Such an interpretation would dovetail nicely with the min_size parameter.

Update:

1/3: I almost have an implementation ready to resolve this specific issue.
2/3: This one is a little more perplexing since there seems to be a spin-lock around the bulk of the contents. However, it is my suspicion that there is an interaction with something that is not protected by pipe's spinlock.  At this point, it is not known what it is, but the first place I plan on investigating is the timer removing something from the pipe's wait queue. And as I write this, I think that I have figured out the key issue--pipes, when they are generating the lists from the wait queues, do not have a lock on those same lists. Thus, they are vulnerable to having those lists corrupted by another processor servicing a timer interrupt that may remove one of the pended threads from the wait queue (and thus the list).
3/3: I think this is directly related to the revelation in 2/3 above.

Although it was not stated in the issue, based on the previous analysis, I think that this problem that you are describing exists on SMP systems and not on those with 1 core/cpu. If it were UP (or SMP with only 1 core), the spinlock would be equivalent to an irq lock, which in turn would prevent ISRs from being serviced (thereby preventing the threads from being removed from the wait queue while a pipe operation was in progress).

I will have to ponder it a bit more to figure out how to resolve this properly.

Thanks for working on this problem. I'm new to Zephyr so I'm not much of a help, but the explanation seems plausible. But please note that the problem was originally seen on an nRF52840, which is a single core CPU. SMP is also not activated. So it seems that it affects non SMP systems as well.

I'm seeing the exact same problem on the exact same (single core) processor. I too use k_pipe_put to write (one byte at a time) from an ISR, which then wakes up a potentially suspended thread that services the pipe data.
So far I can't add any more insight than the quite detailed report on this issue other than "this affects more than one person".
Before finding this bug report I had already figured out that the problem stems from commit f86027f, as on all releases I used prior to that I had no issue.
I am back from holidays and am continuing to work on this.

Thanks for the PR. I just tried the changes (#53634) but the error is still there as described above (error two). Same code to reproduce, same stack trace on error (`prev` is null in `sys_dlist_remove`).

I tested this by using Nordic nRF Connect SDK v2.2.0 (Based on Zephyr cd16a83) and applying the changes manually (because I couldn't work out how to use upstream Zephyr directly) on a nRF52840 single core MCU.

Thanks for the valuable feedback. I had previously tried my testing with a different ARM board (frdm_k64f) using the Zephyr SDK and using irq_offload() to execute test_write_irq() routine and was unable to replicate the issue that way. There are a number of obvious differences between your environment and my own (board, compiler and irq source).

Let's see what else I can come up with to help resolve this bug.

I didn't know about `irq_offload()` and just tested it. Couldn't reproduce the error either, but I did see a difference that could be relevant (or not...): the IRQ priorities* are different. `irq_offload()` uses the SVC IRQ that is set to priority 1 (`SCB.SHPR` value 0x20; set in `arch/arm/include/aarch32/cortex_m/exc.h`), while the UARTE IRQ that I use is priority 3 (`NVIC.IPR` value 0x60). In `arch_irq_lock()` `BASEPRI` is set to priority 2 (value 0x40), so the UARTE IRQ should be blocked, while the SVC IRQ should still be able to run. I would expect that blocking should be safer in this case, but I'm not sure how this could influence spinlocks. Maybe if the BASEPRI gets set while UART IRQ is already running. I tried raising the priority of the UART IRQ, but it seems to deadlock after a while. It's probably not designed to be used that way.

------

*IRQ Priorities on ARM are kind of weird, so here some notes so there is no confusion (on my side):
- Low values are high priorities
- Only top three bits of priority registers are used on nRF52840. So priority 3 corresponds to register value 0x60
Here my currently used config: [.config](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/files/10393284/config.txt)

Although it was a low probability cause of error, I wanted to verify that the interrupt locking is being respected in the pipe code. That is, I wanted to verify that we did not have some weird esoteric case where a timer ISR was interrupting a pipe operation. With some not so fancy flag checking, I was able to confirm to a high enough level of satisfaction that that is not the case. This strongly suggests that there is an algorithmic flaw somewhere in the pipe code. Still digging.

I'm also encountering issue 3 (a pipe fed from an ISR causes an unrelated pipe to wake up with a supposedly full buffer, even though nothing was actually written), #53634 does **not** fix it (at head commit 02c0f49 cherry-picked onto 3.2.0). I have worked around it for now by replacing the ISR pipe with a `k_msgq`.

I may have found the source of the instability.  Both the `z_impl_k_pipe_put()` and `pipe_get_internal()` routines obtain a pointer to the current thread's pipe descriptor `pipe_desc`, which is a structure embedded within the `k_thread` structure. For example, ...

`dest_desc = &_current->pipe_desc;`

This is fine when those routines get invoked at thread-level, but it is not safe to do so from the context of an ISR because this will refer to the thread that was interrupted.

Fixing ....
I have updated #53634 to fix that Sporadic Data Access Violation error. Locally, on my own setup I am no longer able to reproduce the problem as described above after applying that commit.

Nice find! I tested the new changes and the problem seems to be fixed. I can't reproduce the errors anymore either. Not with the code from the issue description and neither with my original code. And this would also explain why unrelated pipes from other threads were also affected. Thanks for fixing this!

Thank you for reporting it! I've also done a bit of a mini-retrospective to determine where I failed in my own personal development process that led to the bug being introduced. I think I have an idea, so hopefully I will be less likely to make the same kind of error again in the future. :)
I have marked this issue as a release blocker for now since it is an quite serious kernel bug.

It appears the first issue reported never had a fix committed before the issue was closed. We are still seeing this behaviour on NRF-Connect SDK 2.5.0 - Zephyr a768a05e6205e415564226543cee67559d15b736

review_comments:
I'm not quite understanding how this acts as a barrier?  I'm guessing the thinking is something like "if another CPU already holds the lock, this forces us to wait until it releases it".  But that doesn't protect against the case where it gets the lock immediately after.

Basically this doesn't feel like a fix to me.  What's the exact sequencing we're trying to protect?  My guess is something needs to be inside a lock that isn't.

Below is the sequence of events.

1. Thread A is in the process of copying a bunch of data for pipe P on core 1.
2. Meanwhile core 2 unpends thread B that was previously waiting on pipe P.
3. Core 2 schedules thread B to run, while thread A is still copying data on core 1.

Both threads A and B then want to simultaneously access thread B's pipe descriptor--A to update it, B to read it. Worse, thread B might execute, block on pipe Q and then thread A starts updating B's pipe descriptor mistakenly thinking that it is safe to do so, when in fact it is now being used by a different pipe altogether.

What we need to do is stop thread B from executing further until the thread A has finished the pipe operation, and the spin lock is the simplest and most effective method I can think of to do it.

So... the scheduler lock is the most contended lock in the whole system.  And this takes it while not only iterating over a list with unbounded length but also calling user-defined callbacks.  That seems like it's just asking for latency bugs.

I see where your concerns are coming from. Walking the wait queue is a functionality to which we do not want to provide too much exposure as it has the potential to be misused. That's one of the reasons why I stuck the prototype in kerenl/include/sched.h--it should imply that it is a restricted operation, and should be used with care. If you like, I can add warnings to the description to make the risks more clear to potential callers (of whom there should be few).

Seems like this is being used to spin and wait for a completion flag effectively, spin locks have some implied irq mask/unmask operations tied to them, do you need that behavior as well or only an atomic cas loop? The comment above doesn't help in terms of the arch irq locking behavior being desired/undesired.

I'm not the happiest with using the spin lock here, but it seemed to be the simplest mechanism to accomplish the following two goals.

 1.  Serve as an indicator that it is safe to continue execution.
 2. Prevent the thread from executing while another core was still in the process of copying the data that the thread had requested.

The biggest downside to this approach that I can see is (and admittedly you may see something more) that the one core is essentially stalled while the other core finishes copying data. However, as an attempt to put this into perspective, I pose the following question ... "Is blocking on the spin lock on the 'tail end' of the pipe operation fundamentally any worse than blocking on a spin lock at the 'front end' of the pipe operation?"

Not understanding the logic change here.  The current (not terribly informative) naming scheme is that z_xxxx() scheduler APIs are (or at least tend to be) synchronized calls and the internal static functions have no prefix and (usually) are expected to be externally synchronized.

And that's true here, where this used to be just a wrapper around the internal function.  But now it's got different behavior, which seems likely to be confusing.

What's the circumstances where you are now able to land here to unpend a thread that isn't actually pended?  That seems like a state management problem somewhere else?

Excellent question--and it is for an SMP case that I did not originally spot when I first re-did the pipes implementation.

Pipe operations essentially act in two stages. In stage one, we create a list of the copying work that needs to be done. In stage two, we perform the copy and unpend an item if necessary once the copying is complete. However, unless I am misunderstanding something, there exists a window of opportunity where a timeout can be processed on another core after the work list has been generated that can cause it to be removed from the wait/pend queue. The pipe's spin-lock does not protect against this.
